title: Concepts are directions you can walk
allegory: A model's state is like your position in a city where every idea is a street running in its own direction: how far along a street you stand reads that idea, and walking along it changes that idea while leaving the cross streets alone.
map: the activation vector in the residual stream
a street running in some direction
how far along that street you stand
reading the concept: the projection x·d
walking a few blocks along the street
asking for the wrong street: 'black or white' instead of 'mine or theirs'
a probe in the wrong basis makes a linear feature look non-linear
credit: The picture of meaning living in directions of a high-dimensional space echoes 3Blue1Brown's deep learning chapters on word embeddings and 'How might LLMs store facts'.

cap.1: Inside a model, every moment is a long list of numbers. Where in those numbers is an idea like 'this square is mine'?
cap.2: An activation is a vector with hundreds of entries. How is a concept, say who owns a board square, stored in it: in one neuron, in a tangle, or somewhere simpler?
cap.3: The linear representation hypothesis: concepts correspond to directions in activation space, so a feature's value is a projection and an intervention is an addition.

cap.1: Picture your spot in a city. Each idea is a street running its own way. How far along a street you stand tells you that idea's value.
cap.2: Each concept is a direction d. Read it by projecting: how far the activation x points along d. Edit it by adding: walk x along d. The cross streets stay put.
cap.3: Feature value = x·d, which is what a linear probe computes; intervention x' = x + αd, which is what a steering vector does. Near-orthogonal directions let many concepts share one space.

cap.1: Two moves. To read an idea, measure how far along its street you are. To change it, walk along that street. Nothing fancier needed.
cap.2: One dot product reads the concept: that's a linear probe. Adding a multiple of the direction edits it: that's a steering vector. Both assume the concept is a direction.
cap.3: If features are linear, probing is a linear classifier on x and intervention is vector addition; if not, both tools can fail or mislead. The hypothesis is what licenses the toolkit.

chapters.name: The Othello twist

right.title: mine vs theirs
lines: stable for the player to move

chapters.verdict: Linear all along, once you ask in the model's own terms.

cap.1: A model that learned Othello seemed to store the board in a tangled way. Asking 'mine or theirs?' instead of 'black or white?' revealed a simple straight line.
cap.2: Li et al. needed a two-layer probe to read OthelloGPT's board. Nanda asked mine versus theirs instead of black versus white: a linear probe worked, and linear edits steered legal moves.
cap.3: Odd- and even-move black−white directions are nearly antipodal (cosine ≈ −1) because the colour label flips each move. In the mine/theirs basis the board is linear, and one edit after layer 4 steers predictions.

cap.1: Reading an idea off a street isn't proof the model uses that street. Walk along it: if the model's behaviour doesn't budge, the street was a leftover.
cap.2: A probe measures what's decodable, not what's used. Pair every probe with the cheapest causal test: add along its direction mid-forward-pass and check the behaviour moves.
cap.3: Probe accuracy can reflect vestigial or downstream features, or an expressive probe computing the feature itself. Evidence strength is inverse to intervention strength: a small linear edit that works is strong evidence.

cap.1: Almost every tool for looking inside AI leans on this one idea. The honest call: treat it as your default, and always check with an edit.
cap.2: Current practice treats concepts as directions: probes, steering vectors and SAEs all assume it. Open question: not every feature need be a simple direction. What you need: default to linear, verify causally.
cap.3: The call: LRH is the working default and holds well enough to power the toolkit; its limits are live research, and linearity is basis-relative (Othello). Read 'needs a non-linear probe' as 'wrong feature?' first.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Read a concept: one dot product
Steer a model: add one vector
Then prove it: the edit must change behaviour

cap.1: If ideas are streets, you can read a model's state with a ruler and nudge it with a step. That's the promise; the check keeps it honest.
cap.2: Probes read concepts, steering vectors change them, SAEs find them by the thousand. All three rest on this hypothesis, which is why every finding gets tested with an intervention.
cap.3: Linear readout plus linear intervention is the core loop for understanding and steering models: find the direction, confirm it causally, then use it to monitor or control behaviour.

coda.title: Walk along concept A: does concept B notice?

params.label: how much B's street overlaps A's

caption.1: Walk along concept A and watch its reading change while concept B's stays still. Then make B's street overlap A's: now every step leaks into B too.
caption.2: Bars are the activation's four numbers. Adding α·d_A moves A's reading by exactly α. With perpendicular streets B is untouched; with overlap o, B moves by α·o: interference.
caption.3: x' = x + αd_A gives x'·d_A = x·d_A + α and x'·d_B = x·d_B + α·cos(A, B). Orthogonality makes edits surgical; superposition packs near-orthogonal directions and accepts some leakage.

where_else: Linear probes: reading one concept with one dot product
Steering vectors: changing behaviour by adding one direction
Sparse autoencoders: finding thousands of such directions at once
Word-vector arithmetic, the classic early sign that meaning can live in directions

hamming.what: The hypothesis that models store concepts as directions in activation space, readable by a projection and editable by an addition.
hamming.when: Whenever you probe, steer or decompose activations: the whole interpretability toolkit leans on it.
hamming.why: Where it holds, simple linear tools can read and control a model's concepts; where it fails they mislead, so every finding gets a causal test.

object.title: The mine-or-theirs cloud
object.subtitle: Activations for one board square as three clouds, split by a straight arrow and a flat sheet.

cap.1: Each dot is one moment's activation, coloured by whether one board square is mine, theirs or blank.
cap.2: Residual-stream activations for one square, labelled by its state.
cap.3: Three classes in activation space; the question is whether they separate linearly.

cap.1: Mine and theirs sit at opposite ends of one straight arrow. That arrow is the concept.
cap.2: The mine − theirs direction separates the two classes.
cap.3: A single direction carries the mine/theirs feature: the claim of the linear representation hypothesis.

cap.1: One flat sheet splits them cleanly. A flat sheet is all a linear probe is.
cap.2: A linear probe is a hyperplane: a direction plus a threshold.
cap.3: Linear separability in the right basis; in the black/white basis the labels would swap sides every move.

cap.1: Blank sits off in its own direction, a second straight line. Two directions per square cover all three states.
cap.2: Blank vs occupied is a second direction, roughly independent of mine vs theirs.
cap.3: Two degrees of freedom per square: blank − (mine + theirs)/2 and mine − theirs, as in the OthelloGPT probe.

cap.1: Walk a dot along the arrow and it crosses the sheet: the model now treats the square as mine. That walk is a steering edit.
cap.2: Adding along the direction moves an activation across the boundary: a linear intervention.
cap.3: If the model uses the direction, x + αd changes downstream behaviour; that causal check is what separates used from merely decodable.

predict.q: What does a linear probe need to separate mine from theirs?

options.t: One flat boundary: a direction and a threshold

predict.why: If the concept is a direction, one projection plus a cutoff reads it.

predict.q: Black-vs-white probe directions for odd and even moves have cosine ≈ −1. What does that tell you?

options.t: The real feature is mine vs theirs; the colour label flips each move
The model doesn't represent the board

predict.why: Opposite directions on alternating moves are exactly what a mine/theirs feature looks like through black/white labels.

predict.q: A probe reads a direction very accurately, but adding along it changes nothing. Conclusion?

options.t: Decodable isn't used: the direction may be vestigial

predict.why: Only a causal edit shows the model actually uses a direction.

object.where: Anywhere a concept is a direction: probes, steering vectors, SAE features, word-vector arithmetic.
